title: How Much Rent Can I Afford? The Housing Squeeze Across Generations
description:
How much rent can I afford is a pressing U.S. pocketbook question as CNBC reports on October 6, 2026 that young voters struggle to afford housing. An October 5 Ramsey Show upload about a 63-year-old unable to afford housing offers a separate older-adult example, not evidence of national prevalence.

For entertainment and informational purposes only. This is not financial, legal, medical, or other professional advice. Consult a qualified professional about your circumstances. We are not responsible for decisions or results based on this video.

scenes.text: America’s median gross rent was $1,406 in 2023—but that isn't an apartment shopping quote.
scenes.subject: apartment leasing office

scenes.text: That's a Census Bureau historical figure. I can't verify today's rental prices here, so let's keep that distinction clear.
scenes.subject: rental apartments

scenes.text: Gross rent combines contract rent with renter-paid utilities and fuels. It describes more than the lease payment alone.
scenes.subject: renter utility bills

scenes.text: Median means the middle, not a recommended budget. Your local apartment search can look very different.
scenes.subject: apartment search

scenes.text: And existing renters aren't necessarily paying what a newly available apartment advertises. Those measurements answer different questions.
scenes.subject: apartment listings

scenes.text: So, how much rent can you afford? Start with a benchmark, then test your actual monthly cash flow.
scenes.subject: household budgeting

scenes.text: The standard housing-cost-burden threshold is more than 30 percent of household income spent on housing costs.
scenes.subject: renter paperwork

visual.headline: Housing-cost-burden threshold
visual.sub: Spending above this share of income

scenes.text: Spending more than 50 percent is considered severe housing cost burden. That's a classification, not a personal spending target.
scenes.subject: kitchen budgeting

visual.headline: Severe housing-cost-burden threshold
visual.sub: Spending above this share of income

scenes.text: Compare those thresholds: above 30 percent signals burden; above 50 percent signals severe burden. Neither guarantees comfort below it.
scenes.subject: budget spreadsheet

scenes.text: These measures generally use income before taxes. But your groceries and bills come out of take-home pay.
scenes.subject: paycheck review

scenes.text: That's why an apartment can pass an income screening and still leave your personal budget feeling tight.
scenes.subject: rental application

visual.headline: Approval isn't the same as affordability

scenes.text: Build your own affordability check backward: start with reliable take-home income, then subtract essential expenses and savings.
scenes.subject: budget notebook

scenes.text: Use income you can reasonably count on. Overtime, tips and freelance work may change from month to month.
scenes.subject: restaurant server

scenes.text: Then list your housing charges separately: base rent, required monthly fees, and utilities that aren't included.
scenes.subject: lease review

scenes.text: Ask which utilities you pay directly. Heating, cooling and water arrangements can differ from building to building.
scenes.subject: apartment thermostat

scenes.text: Check parking, pet charges and required insurance too. A listing's headline price may not capture your entire obligation.
scenes.subject: pet owner

scenes.text: Keep move-in costs separate from recurring costs. A deposit isn't monthly rent, but you still need available cash.
scenes.subject: moving boxes

scenes.text: Before applying, request a written breakdown of required charges. Ask which amounts are refundable and under what conditions.
scenes.subject: leasing agent

scenes.text: A discounted introductory offer deserves another look. Find out what you'll owe after the promotion ends.
scenes.subject: rental advertisement

scenes.text: Compare leases across their full terms, not just the cheapest advertised month. Read how any concession actually works.
scenes.subject: lease documents

scenes.text: Now look beyond the apartment. A cheaper address can bring a longer commute or a different transportation bill.
scenes.subject: car commuter

scenes.text: If public transportation works for your schedule, compare that option. Don't assume every cheaper neighborhood offers practical access.
scenes.subject: bus passenger

scenes.text: For younger adults, the hurdle can include establishing income, building savings and covering that first move all together.
scenes.subject: young adult renter

scenes.text: Living with roommates can divide shared housing costs. But the savings depend on the apartment and your agreement.
scenes.subject: roommates

scenes.text: Talk through rent shares, utilities and shared supplies before moving in. Put the arrangement in writing.
scenes.subject: roommate discussion

scenes.text: Also read the lease's liability terms. Depending on the agreement, another person's missed payment could become your problem.
scenes.subject: roommate lease

scenes.text: For families, affordability involves more than bedrooms. Childcare, school access and work schedules can narrow the available choices.
scenes.subject: family apartment

scenes.text: A lower rent isn't automatically a better deal if the move makes essential childcare harder to arrange.
scenes.subject: childcare pickup

scenes.text: And moving itself takes time: packing, transportation, paperwork and possibly missed work. Include those practical costs in your decision.
scenes.subject: family moving

scenes.text: For older adults, rent has to fit alongside healthcare, transportation and other essentials, sometimes with limited income flexibility.
scenes.subject: older renter

scenes.text: Accessibility matters too. Stairs, bathroom layouts and distance to services can make an inexpensive apartment unsuitable.
scenes.subject: older apartment seeker

scenes.text: These are different pressures, not a competition between generations. Age alone doesn't tell us someone's income or housing options.
scenes.subject: multigenerational family

scenes.text: An individual hardship story can illuminate a problem. It cannot establish how common that problem is nationwide.
scenes.subject: renter interview

scenes.text: The broader squeeze also involves available housing. When suitable homes are scarce, renters have fewer realistic alternatives.
scenes.subject: apartment viewing

scenes.text: New apartments can expand supply, but building takes time. A construction site isn't an available home yet.
scenes.subject: apartment construction workers

scenes.text: And local markets differ. A national rent figure cannot tell you which homes fit your neighborhood and needs.
scenes.subject: neighborhood apartment walk

scenes.text: When comparing current listings, match bedroom count, location, lease length and included utilities. Otherwise, you're comparing different products.
scenes.subject: rental comparison

scenes.text: For your own budget, subtract food, transportation, healthcare and required debt payments before deciding what housing can absorb.
scenes.subject: expense planning

scenes.text: Leave room for irregular expenses too. Car repairs and annual bills don't disappear because they aren't due this month.
scenes.subject: car repair customer

scenes.text: Then stress-test the result. Could you cover housing during a smaller paycheck or an unexpectedly expensive month?
scenes.subject: worker budgeting

scenes.text: If the answer is no, that doesn't mean you failed. It means the proposed rent leaves little flexibility.
scenes.subject: couple reviewing bills

scenes.text: Possible adjustments include sharing housing, changing location or choosing fewer amenities. Each option has real tradeoffs, not guaranteed savings.
scenes.subject: apartment tour couple

scenes.text: If you're renewing, compare the proposed payment with realistic alternatives, including moving costs. Staying can also carry a price.
scenes.subject: lease renewal

scenes.text: Ask about available lease terms and concessions, but don't build your budget around a discount that hasn't been confirmed.
scenes.subject: renter negotiation

scenes.text: For assistance, check your local housing authority. Eligibility, availability and waiting lists vary, so investigate before a deadline.
scenes.subject: housing authority office

scenes.text: If a lease term or charge seems unclear, look for local tenant resources before signing or paying.
scenes.subject: tenant consultation

scenes.text: The key distinction: a national statistic describes housing conditions. Your personal affordability limit describes what your household can sustain.
scenes.subject: household conversation

scenes.text: A useful rent budget includes the whole housing bill, protects essentials and leaves some room for life happening.
scenes.subject: renter monthly planner

scenes.text: Whether you're starting out, raising a family or retired, the goal is a payment your actual life can support.
scenes.subject: apartment residents

scenes.text: What share of your take-home pay goes to rent, and do you live alone or split the cost? Comment below, and like the video.
